note: Concept DAG of the course, built from first principles: a node is a mental model (kind=concept) or a decision rule/technique that applies mental models (kind=practice); deps lists what you must understand first. Rules: guide/DAG.md. The page is generated by tools/dag.py.

tiers.Basic: Can be stated in one sentence and understood from everyday experience or one prerequisite; without it, most of what follows cannot be read
tiers.Intermediate: Needs two or more prerequisites held at once; usually a design decision or a cost calculation
tiers.Expert: Goes inside the mechanism (formulas, hardware units, algorithms) or judges the validity of research results; skippable if you do not build serving, harnesses or evals yourself, because upstream judgments do not depend on it

nodes.name: The model is a function: a token sequence in, a probability distribution over the next token out; it keeps nothing between calls, and text is generated by calling it again and again
nodes.short: The model is a next-token function
nodes.why: Root. Everything in the course follows from this one object: sampling comes from the distribution, the context from the lack of memory, prefill and decode from calling it once per token, and cost from paying per call.

nodes.name: Output is sampled from the distribution: the same input does not give the same output; temperature, top-k and top-p shape the draw and also change the output length
nodes.why: From the next-token function: the function returns a distribution and the system draws one token from it. That draw is where the randomness enters, and why testing, verification and evaluation cannot assume determinism. Temperature and top-p only change the shape of the draw.

nodes.name: Tokens: a tokenizer cuts text into tokens (BPE merges from bytes up); tokens are the unit of length, cost and compute; Traditional Chinese is about 0.7–0.9 tokens per character
nodes.why: From the next-token function: the function's input and output are tokens, not characters, so every budget in the course (context length, KV cache, price) is counted in tokens. How many tokens a Chinese sentence becomes is decided by the vocabulary.

nodes.name: Temperature 0 does not guarantee identical output: floating-point summation order and batch composition change the 7th significant digit
nodes.why: From sampling and batching: even when the top score is always taken, the order of parallel sums on the GPU changes with who else is in the batch, and floating-point error swaps two close scores. Determinism has to come from the system layer, not from temperature.

nodes.name: The agent loop: a program calls the model, executes the step it proposes, appends the result and calls again; the model proposes, the program acts; one task is a chain of calls
nodes.why: From the next-token function: because the function remembers nothing, something outside it has to keep the task going. That program is the loop, and a task becomes a chain of many calls. L1 describes the chain as a workload, L2 as the mechanism inside Claude Code.

nodes.name: The context is the model's whole world: one text sequence holding instructions, history, tool output and memory, rebuilt and resent in full on every call, with nothing marking where each part came from
nodes.short: The context is the model's world
nodes.why: From the agent loop: the function has no memory, so each call must carry everything, and the loop resends the growing sequence every turn. Three consequences follow: every token is paid for again each turn (money, latency, attention), the sequence only grows, and the model cannot tell an instruction from data by where it came from.

nodes.name: A tool is a text interface: the model sees a name, a description and a parameter schema; it emits a call as text; the program executes it and the result goes into the context
nodes.why: From the context: the model never runs anything. It reads tool definitions as text, proposes a call as text, and gets the result back as more context. So tool output is the next turn's input, and anything a tool can read, the model reads.

nodes.name: The harness: the program around the model (loop, tools, memory, permissions) decides most of the behavior; it is the OS of a new computer that makes mistakes
nodes.why: From the agent loop and sampling: the model errs and has no state, so a surrounding layer has to manage memory, permissions and tools for it, the way an OS manages hardware. Most product differences live in this layer.

nodes.name: Two kinds of control: an instruction in the context is followed probabilistically; code in the harness runs every time. Anything that must be guaranteed goes in code
nodes.why: From the harness (and, behind it, sampling): a rule in the prompt is one more input to a sampled function, so it is followed only sometimes; a check in the harness is ordinary software and runs every time. Guarantees can only live in the latter.

nodes.name: The stack: each layer moves one term of the goal, problems cross layers, and you cannot optimize what you cannot see
nodes.why: From the harness and cost per successful task: the goal has several terms and each layer (agent, harness, serving, model, runtime, hardware) moves one of them, so choosing which layer to touch needs the goal first. Problems cross layers, so you need traces to see them.

nodes.name: Permissions: rules come before modes and autonomy must match risk; rules only match strings, only a sandbox limits the process
nodes.why: From guarantees in code: blocking dangerous actions must rely on harness rules, not the prompt; but rules only match command strings, and only a sandbox truly limits the process, so the three layers stack and autonomy is set to match the risk.

nodes.name: Prompt injection: the model cannot tell instructions from data and filtering does not work; config files in the repo and text returned by other agents are attack surface
nodes.why: From the context and guarantees in code: the context carries no marker of where text came from, so anything a tool reads sits beside the user's instructions and the model cannot tell them apart. The defense cannot be asking the model to filter; it must be structural: limit what the agent can reach. L5's 'returned text is untrusted too' is the same thing with several agents.

nodes.name: Event hooks: code attached to events of the loop; it always runs, but only does what its matching logic says. Superpowers and mattpocock/skills show the choice: enforce a written process with a hook, or hand the guarantee to a person
nodes.why: From guarantees in code: a hook is how a guarantee becomes code, attached to loop events such as 'before a tool runs'. The matching logic is yours, so a wrong pattern lets things through. Superpowers and mattpocock/skills both write a development process into skills (text); only one adds hooks to enforce it.

nodes.name: External tool servers (MCP): tools provided by another process or service; to the model they look exactly like built-in tools, but they run outside with your credentials
nodes.why: From a tool is three strings and permissions: an MCP server is just a source of tool definitions in the same text form, so the model treats them like Read or Bash. The difference is where they run and whose credentials they carry, so judge them with the permissions lens.

nodes.name: Plugins: package skills, hooks, MCP and subagents so others can install them; installing one runs someone else's code
nodes.why: From event hooks, external tool servers and keep it out until needed: a plugin bundles skills, hooks and MCP servers so others can install them in one step. Its risk is the sum of the parts: hooks and servers run someone else's code with your permissions.

nodes.name: Harness architecture: where the boundary goes depends on what to isolate and what must outlive a session; three architectures differ in which boundary a call crosses; ask three questions, do not count agents
nodes.why: From teams and scripted workflows and permissions: loop, tools and state can live in one process, in separate processes or in a remote service; the farther the boundary, the more isolation and persistence, at the price of crossing it on every call. What to isolate and what must survive a session decide where it goes.

nodes.name: Keep it out until needed: admit only what the turn needs, keep the rest outside and load it on demand (offloading; skills do this for procedures: a one-line description stays resident, the body loads on use)
nodes.why: From the context: whatever enters is paid for every turn, so the cheapest management happens at the door. Read only the files needed, truncate tool output, keep procedures and data in files and load them when a step calls for them. The price of loading on demand is recall: the model must notice it needs the thing, and sometimes it does not.

nodes.name: Context structure: ten slots, and only a stable head saves money
nodes.short: Keep the head of context stable
nodes.why: From prefix cache: the cache only matches the identical leading segment, so the system prompt and tool definitions go first and must not change, while anything volatile goes after. Wrong order means recomputing every turn.

nodes.name: What already got in: delete by rule first (transformation), summarize last (compaction); keep the record separate from what the model sees
nodes.why: From keep it out until needed and prefix cache: what you could not keep out can be trimmed by rule, deleting old tool output without an LLM and without loss; compaction summarizes with an LLM and is lossy, so it comes last. Both edit the middle of the context, so you need to know where the cache stops matching.

nodes.name: Five tool-design principles: errors must teach, idempotent by default, output need not enter context; is a shell alone enough?
nodes.why: From a tool is three strings and failure is normal: since output is context, error messages must be written so the model can correct itself; since calls get retried, actions must be idempotent; large outputs can be processed outside (code execution) before entering context.

nodes.name: Execution: the shell is the most powerful and all protection lives in the harness; if the shell can do everything, why dedicated read and edit tools?
nodes.why: From tool principles and permissions: a shell can do anything, so it can break anything, and the only limit is the harness's permission rules. Dedicated tools buy controlled output, visible failure and fewer tokens.

nodes.name: Search: grep first, switch only when you cannot guess the name (glob, semantic search, repo map, extrinsic signals, LSP)
nodes.why: From tool principles: the five ways to find code differ in cost, in whether they need an index and in whether results go stale. grep costs nothing and never goes stale, so it comes first; switch to meaning- or symbol-based search only when you cannot guess the name.

nodes.name: Edit: whether failure is visible matters as much as saving tokens (full rewrite, unified diff, search/replace, AST)
nodes.why: From tool principles: the four edit formats differ in token use and in how they fail. search/replace fails loudly when the target is missing; a diff with wrong line numbers silently edits the wrong place, so saving tokens is not the first concern.

nodes.name: Prompting: tricks expire, principles do not
nodes.why: From sampling and the context: a prompt trick tunes the model's distribution and dies with the next model. What lasts: give enough context, state the goal, show examples.

nodes.name: When results are poor, check context and harness before changing the model; read multipliers with their conditions; fix the harness when evaluating
nodes.why: From five layers of failure and the context: most of the layers you can change are context and harness, and the same model with a different harness differs several-fold in success rate. So when results are poor, suspect the layers you control before switching the model, and hold the harness fixed when you evaluate.

nodes.name: Secrets: anything that entered the context stays in the transcript; why logs carry keys
nodes.why: From a tool is three strings: the .env a tool read and the token a command printed are in the context, and the harness saves every turn's context as a transcript. So keep secrets out of tool reach rather than scrubbing logs afterwards.

nodes.name: Sessions: one session, one job, state in files; long sessions lose context to compaction; when stuck, give evidence, not frustration
nodes.why: From checkpoints and limits and delete by rule: a long session eventually compacts and the summary is lossy, so writing progress to files and keeping one job per session is doing your own checkpointing. When stuck, pasting the error beats saying 'still broken'.

nodes.name: Three axes of scaling — more agents, longer runs, stronger steps — and each buys one thing only
nodes.why: From the agent loop: a chain can be made longer (run longer), thicker (a stronger model per step) or multiplied (more agents). The three buy different things; separate them before discussing how to scale.

nodes.name: The ceiling: 16 agents are not 16× faster; if the task cannot be split, adding agents does nothing, and coordination takes time too
nodes.why: From the three axes: more chains only speed up the part that can run in parallel; the serial part (planning, integration, review) stays, so speedup has a ceiling. This is Amdahl's law.

nodes.name: People: how many agents you can run is set by your review speed; the more agents do, the fewer errors humans catch
nodes.why: From human time and Amdahl's ceiling: the slowest serial step is usually human review, so the agent count is capped at m ÷ r (output rate over review rate). L11's assignment data shows the same thing: the more agents do, the less humans look. dsh-superagent takes the consequence seriously and builds the architecture around saving human attention: the main session only routes, workers do the work, results pass verification before reaching a person.

nodes.name: Autonomy is set by verifiability: write 'done' as a checkable condition; when the agent says 'done' that is a claim, so look for evidence
nodes.why: From human review is the bottleneck and the verification loop: when human review is too slow, how far you can let go depends on programmatic verification standing in for the human; only a checkable goal (/goal, tests) lets an agent run on its own. L11 turns this into concrete practice before starting and when finishing.

nodes.name: Parallel agents need isolated state: a git worktree isolates only files; ports, databases and main still collide; long runs must survive the session
nodes.why: From the three axes of scaling and agents share only text: running agents side by side is easy, but they share the machine. A worktree separates files and nothing else, so beyond a few agents you need separate environments, and long runs need somewhere to resume from. The assignments hit exactly this.

nodes.name: Teams and workflows: use a team only when agents need to discuss, a script when conversation cannot coordinate; 16 agents need no lead if tests and git are in place
nodes.why: From agents share only text and verification sets autonomy: a team is worth it only when agents must talk back and forth; when the parallel count outgrows conversation, a script and git become the coordinator, provided tests accept each agent's work.

nodes.name: Separate contexts: another agent is another context; agents share nothing but text, so delegating and reporting back are both lossy summaries (subagents are the simplest case)
nodes.why: From the context: an agent is one context plus one loop, so a second agent is a second, disconnected context. Everything between them is a text message, which loses background on the way out and detail on the way back. Every benefit and every cost of splitting work comes from this.

nodes.name: The most important judgment: most tasks should not be split; splitting helps only when subtasks can proceed independently
nodes.short: Most tasks should not be split
nodes.why: From Amdahl's ceiling and agents share only text: a task whose steps depend on each other gains no parallelism from splitting but still pays the lossy hand-off, so the default is not to split.

nodes.name: The most useful boundary: reads can run in parallel, writes stay on one line; writer plus reviewer is the pattern to learn; verification matters more than architecture
nodes.why: From most tasks should not be split and verification sets autonomy: read-only agents only accumulate findings, so they can run together; writing agents carry unspoken decisions, and two halves written separately will conflict. Architecture names matter less than whether a reviewer verifies.

nodes.name: Delegation: the worker's whole world is that prompt; how fine to split, along which seams, and always set a limit
nodes.why: From agents share only text: the agent taking over has none of your context; whatever the task description leaves out, it does not know. So cut along clear boundaries and give a limit on steps and budget.

nodes.name: Reporting back: the message carries only the claim and the evidence; the raw output goes to a file
nodes.why: From agents share only text: returning the full output blows up the main conversation's context, while returning only a conclusion cannot be checked. So the message carries a claim plus checkable evidence (file paths, test results) and the raw text stays in a file.

nodes.name: After sending: timeouts, idempotency and partial failure; you cannot tell slow from dead
nodes.why: From failure is normal and agents share only text: a dispatched agent may be slow, dead or half-done, and silence does not tell you which. So set timeouts, and make re-dispatch safe by making actions idempotent.

nodes.name: State and time: every agent's context is a copy that goes stale; consistency, CAP, no global clock, observability
nodes.why: From agents share only text and failure is normal: when shared data changes, every agent's earlier copy in context is stale, which is the consistency problem of distributed systems. Under a partition CAP says you keep one side, timestamps cannot order events, and traces stitch the logs together.

nodes.name: Failure is normal: in a single run, fear the tools before the GPU; you cannot tell slow from dead
nodes.why: From the agent loop: a chain passes through many tool calls and network hops, any of which can be slow or dead, and when no reply comes you cannot tell which. GPU failures are what long training runs worry about first, not agents.

nodes.name: Errors compound: 95% per step leaves 8% after 50 steps, but both premises of the formula fail in real runs
nodes.why: From sampling and the agent loop: every step has an error rate and a long chain multiplies them. But real runs detect and fix errors, so pⁿ is not an upper bound; the three levers (steps, per-step success, catching errors) are what matter.

nodes.name: Verification: without a stronger model, 8% can become 88%; checks must really catch errors, come early, and not rely on the model's self-discipline
nodes.why: From errors compound and guarantees in code: put a check that really catches errors after each step and retry, and overall success stops being a product of per-step rates. The check must be code (tests, types, lint), not asking the model 'are you sure?'.

nodes.name: Checkpoints and limits: how far to roll back on failure, what to save (context too), commit before irreversible actions, and how much to spend at most
nodes.why: From the verification loop and failure is normal: once a check catches an error you roll back to a verified state and retry, so you need checkpoints (git for files, and the context must roll back too); irreversible actions like deleting or sending need an escape route first; keep failing and you must stop. L11's 'commit first' is the implementation.

nodes.name: Failure has layers: one symptom, five sources (model, prompt, tool, environment, task); fix at the source layer; without records you do not know what to change
nodes.why: From the stack and a score is the whole system: a failed run has one symptom but five possible sources (model, prompt, tool, environment, task), each on a different layer. Find the first failing step, decide which layer it belongs to, and fix there. This needs a complete trace.

nodes.name: Persistent instructions and memory: text written once and injected into the context in every later session (CLAUDE.md, auto memory); it pays rent every turn, nobody tells you when it has expired, and a wrong line is worse than a missing one
nodes.why: From the context and guarantees in code: whatever is saved for later sessions becomes context again, so every line costs money and attention on every turn and is followed only probabilistically. Human-written instruction files and model-written memory are the same object with different authors; both need a rule for what is worth writing, and a wrong line misleads every turn.

nodes.name: Time and source: valid time and provenance not stored at write time cannot be recovered; summarization is the riskiest write; forgetting is a first-class operation
nodes.why: From persistent text pays rent: to judge whether a saved line can still be trusted you need to know when it held and who said it, and both are only available at write time. Memories the model summarized itself have the model as their source; flag them most and make them deletable.

nodes.name: Retrieval: semantic similarity is one signal of five; filter vs. rank differ in consequences; what must be present should not depend on retrieval; k is a context budget
nodes.why: From persistent text pays rent and keep it out until needed: every retrieval spends context budget, so k must be small and ranked. Similarity alone misses time, source and frequency; what must always be present stays resident.

nodes.name: Where to put it: derive the backend from how you will query; start with files, measure the scores yourself
nodes.why: From retrieval, valid time and provenance, and change one thing at a time: pick a backend only after you know how you will query and which fields to store. Files are the simplest and diffable; a vector store's benefit counts only after you measure it on your own tasks.

nodes.name: Security: memory lets an injection outlive a session; none of the four entry paths looks like 'writing memory'
nodes.why: From prompt injection and persistent text pays rent: an injection used to affect one conversation; once written into memory it loads every time. So the write step needs a defense that does not rely on the model's judgment.

nodes.name: Testing needs two layers: ordinary tests for the deterministic parts, statistics for the probabilistic parts
nodes.why: From guarantees in code: the deterministic parts of a harness can be tested like any software; the parts that pass through the model are probabilistic, so the same input gives different outputs and you can only run many times and look at the rate.

nodes.name: The basic fact: a score is the output of the whole system (model, harness, environment, grader); hold the rest fixed when comparing
nodes.short: A score is the whole system
nodes.why: From the harness is the OS: what runs a benchmark is not just the model; harness, tools, environment and grader all shape the result. The same model scores very differently in a different harness, so first ask 'whose score?'.

nodes.name: Public scores cannot answer 'can we ship': actions and grader may differ from yours, benchmarks have no users, and damage along the way is not penalized
nodes.why: From a score is the whole system and cost per successful task: a benchmark fixes one harness and one grader, unlike your production setting; it also ignores cost, human time and collateral damage, so it cannot say whether you can ship.

nodes.name: Metrics: one success rate hides stability and cost; pass@k vs. pass^k; cost per successful task; Pareto for several dimensions
nodes.why: From cost per successful task (and, behind it, sampling): because runs vary, one item has to be run k times, and 'at least one success' (pass@k) and 'every run succeeds' (pass^k) are different numbers; whether you can retry decides which one to read. Add cost per successful task and you have a score you can decide on.

nodes.name: Noise: a few points of difference is often luck; item count sets precision, infrastructure is noise too, compare versions paired
nodes.why: From metrics: each item's result is a sample, and with few items the confidence interval is wide; harness and environment differences leak into the score too. Compare two versions on the same items in the same environment, paired.

nodes.name: Leakage: answers can enter from anywhere in the stack (training data, the agent finding them, git history)
nodes.why: From a score is the whole system: an agent with tools can find answers in its environment (git log, the web, caches), so training data is not the only entry. The environment must be resettable and you must check what the agent can reach.

nodes.name: Graders: they misjudge, and agents exploit them; passing tests is not being done; write tests for the grader
nodes.why: From a score is the whole system and the verification loop: the grader is part of the system, and if it misjudges the score is wrong; agents optimize against grader loopholes, so checks must really catch errors and the grader itself must be tested.

nodes.name: Saturation: benchmarks are consumables; the next version takes over; your own item set burns out faster
nodes.why: From what public scores cannot tell and leakage: once public, a benchmark enters training data and gets optimized against, and a saturated score no longer separates abilities. Your own set, run repeatedly by your own agent, saturates faster.

nodes.name: Building an eval: start from real failures; a resettable environment with answers out of reach; three grader layers; partial credit for long tasks
nodes.why: From graders are fallible, leakage and noise: your own eval must avoid these three traps. Items come from real failures, the environment is resettable with answers hidden, graders come in three layers (code, LLM, human), and there are enough items to see a difference.

nodes.name: Deciding with evals: three piles of items, change one thing at a time against a baseline; ship conditions in CI; a jump in score is a reason for suspicion
nodes.short: Change one thing at a time
nodes.why: From build evals from real failures: with your own item set, every prompt, model or tool change happens one at a time, compared against the baseline on the same items; the difference must exceed the noise. L11's experimental discipline is the same thing.

nodes.name: Claude Code changes under your feet: numbers measured through it mix in its own changes; safety nets tied to a specific tool fail silently
nodes.why: From a score is the whole system and permissions: the harness is part of the score, and when it auto-updates the difference you measured may be its change; a permission rule tied to a tool name dies silently when the tool is renamed.

nodes.name: The goal is not throughput but cost per successful task
nodes.why: From the agent loop and sampling: a task is many calls and some of them fail, so the denominator must be tasks that succeeded, with the failed attempts folded into the price. Tokens/sec sees neither.

nodes.name: The missing term in the goal: human time; when someone is waiting, the batching answer flips
nodes.why: From cost per successful task and batching: a larger batch saves GPU but makes the waiting person wait longer; once their hourly cost is in the formula the conclusion reverses. Large batches are for work nobody is waiting on.

nodes.name: The cost formula: six multipliers, and the denominator counts successful tasks; compare marginal cost, not only the average
nodes.why: From cost per successful task and the context: a task costs tasks × turns per task × steps per turn × tokens per step × price, divided by the success rate. Resent context is most of tokens per step.

nodes.name: Where the money goes: mostly re-reading context; three token types with volume and price in opposite directions; resent volume grows with the square of the turn count
nodes.why: From the cost formula: every step resends the whole context, so input tokens far outnumber output tokens; output is pricier per token but small in volume. Save on input first, and note that each step gets dearer as the context grows. The Caveman case shows the trap: a skill can only change the model's output style, while the input side can only be rewritten before the request leaves, which only a proxy can do.

nodes.name: Prompt cache: it matches only the prefix; one different character and everything after it is recomputed; uncached tokens cost 12–50×; batch API for work that can wait
nodes.why: From the KV cache and the context: the head of each turn's resent context is nearly identical, and the serving side keeps the computed KV cache, so an identical prefix need not be recomputed. That is why it is cheap, and why it only matches from the very start.

nodes.name: Net savings: every saving has a reverse cost; compaction pays back after N steps; measure only on the same task set; optimization is a loop
nodes.why: From where the money goes, delete by rule, and change one thing at a time: compaction saves tokens on later steps but pays for a summary and may drop information that fails the task. The net effect is known only after running the same task set.

nodes.name: Fewer steps: first ask whether this step needs an LLM at all, then cut turns and steps; reusing plans and skills pays off only for repeated tasks
nodes.why: From where the money goes and guarantees in code: steps and turns are multipliers in the formula. Doing deterministic steps in code without an LLM, and doing several actions in one call, both cut multipliers.

nodes.name: Model, effort and output: only steps that are cheap to get wrong deserve a smaller model; switch models while the context is small; thinking counts as output
nodes.why: From where the money goes, prefix cache and errors compound: a smaller model saves on price but one wrong step drags the whole chain, so switch only on steps that are cheap to get wrong; switching invalidates the cache, so do it while the context is small.

nodes.name: Limits: runaway tasks need someone to call a stop; four caps with numbers taken from traces; progress checks before the cap
nodes.why: From checkpoints and limits and the cost formula: failed tasks tend to run longest and cost most, so turns, tokens, time and money all need caps, with numbers from the distribution in historical traces; an earlier signal is a progress check.

nodes.name: Completion time follows the critical path, money follows everything; time is usually spent in tools; where each speedup sends the money; speculation
nodes.why: From Amdahl's ceiling, where the money goes and human time: completion time is set by the longest dependent chain; parallelism shortens it but the total cost stays or rises. Measure first: time usually goes to tools, not the model.

nodes.name: Life of a request: prefill reads the whole input at once, decode emits one token at a time, and the length is unknown in advance
nodes.why: Root. The model computes one next token at a time: first it processes the whole input (prefill), then generates token by token (decode). L1 covers what this does to latency, L9 how a request flows — the same concept.

nodes.name: Batching: compute many requests together — the GPU gets faster, each request gets slower; every step re-decides who gets on
nodes.why: From prefill and decode and GPUs trade latency for throughput: a decode step computes one token, far too little to fill hardware built for volume, so many users' next steps are computed together. The price is that each step waits for everyone else, and the batch is rebuilt every step as requests finish.

nodes.name: KV cache: what prefill computed is kept for decode; it grows linearly with length, and moving it is the real bottleneck
nodes.why: From prefill and decode: every decode step needs intermediate values from all previous tokens; without storing them you would recompute them, so they stay in GPU memory. How big it is and where it lives is the first serving decision.

nodes.name: An agent's KV cache sits idle: the idle time comes from humans, the moment to move it is the turn boundary, full memory falls off a cliff, and the KV cache becomes a storage tier
nodes.short: KV cache as a storage tier
nodes.why: From KV cache and the agent loop: an agent conversation has many turns, and between them it waits on a tool or a person while the KV cache occupies memory nobody uses. So it gets moved somewhere cheaper and becomes a tier that is swapped in and out.

nodes.name: Different bottlenecks, different GPUs: run prefill and decode on separate machines
nodes.why: From the three numbers: prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so on one card they get in each other's way. Serving systems split them across GPUs and move the KV cache between them.

nodes.name: Five assumptions flipped: the parts are the same as in classic systems, the workload is not
nodes.why: Summary node: classic systems assume short requests, no state, determinism, rare failures and stable architectures; running LLMs flips all five. They come from the KV cache (and prefill/decode behind it), sampling and failure as normal.

nodes.name: The model's skeleton: a stack of identical blocks; parameters are the numbers in matrices; each token becomes a vector; nearly all compute is matrix multiplication
nodes.why: From prefill and decode: to know what 'compute the next token' means on hardware, you need to know that the model is dozens of identical blocks, each a few matrix multiplications. Parameter count and FLOPs follow from here.

nodes.name: Attention: every new token reads all previous K and V; n tokens give n² scores; multi-head, GQA
nodes.why: From the model's skeleton: attention is the only part of a block that looks at earlier tokens; each token produces Q, K and V vectors, and each new token scores against all previous K. That is where the n² comes from, and the K and V are what a KV cache stores. GQA shares one K/V set across several heads to shrink it.

nodes.name: Three numbers: weights bound memory and decode, FLOPs bound prefill, KV cache bounds users and length; the agent's ledger: compute can be saved, memory cannot
nodes.why: From attention, batching and the KV cache: the parameter count sets how many bytes each step reads from memory, FLOPs set how long prefill takes, the KV cache sets how many users and how long a context fit. Map the three numbers to a GPU's three specs and you know where it is bound.

nodes.name: MoE: memory counts all parameters, compute counts only what each token uses; in decode, bigger batches read more experts
nodes.why: From the three numbers: MoE splits the FFN into many experts and each token visits a few, so FLOPs follow the active parameters while memory follows all of them, two separate ledgers. This changes the prefill and decode bottlenecks.

nodes.name: Changing the KV cache architecture: sliding window, MLA, linear attention, state-space models, sparse attention; the direction is hybrid
nodes.why: From the three numbers: the KV cache grows linearly because of attention's structure, so shrinking it means changing attention: look only at recent tokens, compress what each token stores, or replace it with a fixed-size state. Each trades precision for memory.

nodes.name: Self-hostable models: KV cache per token differs by up to 13×, and one formula over config.json gives it
nodes.why: From architectures that shrink KV cache: layers × KV heads × head dim × 2 × precision is the bytes per token. GQA, MLA and sliding window each change one term, so when choosing a model this number matters as much as the parameter count.

nodes.name: GPU design: thousands of simple cores trade latency for throughput; latency and throughput are two different goals
nodes.why: Root. A GPU gives up single-core speed for volume. This trade-off explains roofline, batching, and what every later kernel optimization is chasing.

nodes.name: Roofline: a kernel's time is set by the slower side (compute or memory bandwidth); arithmetic intensity and the ridge point
nodes.why: From GPUs trade latency for throughput: a GPU has two ceilings, FLOPs per second and bytes per second from memory. How many operations a kernel does per byte read (arithmetic intensity) decides which ceiling it hits.

nodes.name: Decode: batch 1 uses 0.5% of the compute; batching raises the weights' intensity but not attention's; a longer context makes every step slower
nodes.why: From roofline and the three numbers: a decode step uses each weight once, so intensity is tiny and it hits memory bandwidth. Computing many users together reuses each weight, but each user's KV cache is read separately, so attention's intensity does not rise.

nodes.name: Measurement: nvidia-smi's 100% only means a kernel is running; MFU for compute, MBU for bandwidth; look at the timeline before the kernel
nodes.why: From decode on the roofline: once you know which ceiling you should be hitting, you can judge whether a measurement is saturated, MFU for prefill and MBU for decode. 100% utilization says nothing about either ceiling.

nodes.name: Inside the chip: SMs, warps and SIMT, Tensor Cores, a memory hierarchy that is faster and smaller the closer it is; Little's law says bandwidth needs bytes in flight
nodes.why: From roofline: how thousands of cores are organized (SMs, warps of 32 threads), why matrix multiplication is fast (Tensor Cores), why memory needs parallelism to keep up (Little's law). This is the hardware behind the two roofline lines.

nodes.name: GPU programming: write for one thread, start at the highest abstraction; graph compilers, tile languages; five layers with more control and more cost the lower you go
nodes.why: From inside the chip: knowing that the hardware is warps and SMs explains why a kernel is 'written for one thread, run on thousands'. Compilers and tile languages do that mapping for you.

nodes.name: Inside a kernel: move less data; fusion keeps intermediates off HBM; FlashAttention computes block by block, and online softmax gets it right without seeing the full row
nodes.why: From attention and inside the chip: writing attention's n×n score matrix to HBM and reading it back is pure data movement. FlashAttention tiles it and finishes on-chip, which is the roofline's 'raise intensity' applied to attention.

nodes.name: Between kernels: remove idle time across SMs, launches and GPUs; split-KV, CUDA Graphs, megakernels, overlapping communication with compute; most teams pick an engine
nodes.why: From FlashAttention, GPU programming and decode on the roofline: with a kernel written, time still leaks in the last wave that uses a fraction of the SMs, in the gaps between launches, and in waiting on inter-GPU communication. Decode attention must be split along the KV cache to fill the SMs.

nodes.name: AI-written kernels: prove it correct before believing it is fast; bugs cluster in four places; speed of light is the roofline's lower bound on time
nodes.why: From GPU programming and the verification loop: AI-generated kernels fail on boundaries, precision and synchronization, and they game benchmarks. Accept one by proving correctness against a reference first, then compare its speed with the roofline's lower bound.

nodes.name: Beyond one card: scale-up vs. scale-out; leaving the machine costs an order of magnitude; 16K GPUs fail about every 3 hours; a 120 kW rack needs liquid cooling
nodes.why: From GPUs trade latency for throughput and failure is normal: when one card is not enough you go across cards and machines, losing an order of magnitude of bandwidth per hop; more cards fail more often, and power and cooling become real limits.

kinds.concept: A mental model: a way the system behaves that you hold in your head and that stays true across products (the loop, the context, the KV cache, Amdahl's ceiling). Concepts form the skeleton of the DAG and never depend on practices.
kinds.practice: A decision rule, technique or worked case that applies concepts (grep first, checkpoints and limits, FlashAttention, the Caveman case). Practices depend on concepts and on other practices.
